gloss: A large vein in the neck that carries blood back down from the head.
examples: The blade missed his *jugular* by an inch.
The medic pressed two fingers to the boy's *jugular*.
In a debate she always goes for the *jugular*.

gloss: A coin-operated machine in a bar or diner that plays songs you pick.
examples: Somebody put five dollars in the *jukebox*.
The diner still has a working *jukebox* in the corner.
Half the songs on that *jukebox* are from the sixties.

gloss: An untidy mix of different things thrown together.
examples: The drawer is a *jumble* of cords and old chargers.
Her notes were a *jumble* of half-finished sentences.
He pulled a *jumble* of clothes out of the dryer.

gloss: An act of pushing yourself off the ground into the air, or a sudden rise in an amount.
examples: He cleared the fence in one *jump*.
She won the meet with a *jump* of six feet.
There was a sharp *jump* in gas prices last month.

gloss: A sleeveless dress worn over a blouse or sweater.
examples: She wore a corduroy *jumper* over a white turtleneck.
The school uniform is a navy *jumper* and knee socks.
Both *jumpers* were on the clearance rack.
contrast: US/UK split: in American English a *jumper* is a sleeveless dress; in British English it means a sweater.

gloss: A particular point in time, especially an important one in a series of events.
examples: At this *juncture* we can't afford to lose another supplier.
The talks reached a critical *juncture* on Friday.
This is a delicate *juncture* in the investigation.

gloss: An evergreen shrub or small tree with berry-like cones used to flavor gin.
examples: A row of *junipers* lines the driveway.
Gin gets its flavor from *juniper* berries.
He trimmed the *juniper* by the front steps.

gloss: An expert in law, especially a judge or a legal scholar.
examples: She was one of the most respected *jurists* of her generation.
The panel included two *jurists* and a historian.
A well-known *jurist* wrote the introduction to the casebook.

gloss: A young person who is not yet legally an adult.
examples: Two *juveniles* were arrested at the scene.
The center houses *juveniles* awaiting trial.
As a *juvenile*, he was released to his parents.

gloss: Pieces of meat and vegetables grilled on a skewer.
examples: We grilled chicken *kabobs* on the deck.
Each *kabob* had peppers and onions between the chunks of lamb.
The place downtown does a good beef *kabob*.
contrast: Also spelled *kebab* or *kebob*; all three are said kuh-BAHB.

gloss: A tube you look through that shows changing colored patterns as you turn it.
examples: Every kid at the party got a *kaleidoscope*.
She turned the *kaleidoscope* slowly and watched the shapes fall apart.
The market was a *kaleidoscope* of color and noise.

gloss: A pilot who deliberately crashes a plane into a target, or the plane itself.
examples: A *kamikaze* hit the carrier's deck.
The navy lost two ships to *kamikazes* that week.
He drives like a *kamikaze*.

gloss: Entertainment in which people sing along to recorded backing music.
examples: We did *karaoke* at a bar downtown.
There's *karaoke* every Thursday night.
She only sings *karaoke* after two drinks.
contrast: Americans say it in four syllables, keh-ree-OH-kee, not the way it sounds in Japanese.

gloss: A small toy instrument that buzzes when you hum into it.
examples: Each kid got a paper hat and a *kazoo*.
He played the melody on a *kazoo*.
Somebody in the back was blowing a *kazoo* through the whole speech.

gloss: A small falcon that hovers in the air while hunting.
examples: A *kestrel* was hovering over the field.
*Kestrels* nest in the barn every spring.
We watched a *kestrel* drop onto a mouse in the grass.

gloss: A type of organic compound; in the body, one of the substances made when fat is burned for energy.
examples: The test strip turns purple if there are *ketones* in your urine.
On a low-carb diet the body starts producing *ketones*.
Acetone is the simplest *ketone*.

gloss: A musician who plays an electronic keyboard in a band.
examples: The band is looking for a *keyboardist*.
Their *keyboardist* writes most of the songs.
Two *keyboardists* traded solos during the encore.

gloss: The main speech at a conference, or the central idea running through something.
examples: She's giving the *keynote* at the developers' conference.
Fairness was the *keynote* of his whole campaign.
Both *keynotes* were streamed live.

gloss: A single press of a key on a keyboard.
examples: The shortcut saves you about ten *keystrokes*.
The software logs every *keystroke*.
One wrong *keystroke* deleted the whole file.

gloss: A blow or push made with the foot.
examples: The goalie stopped the *kick* with one hand.
He gave the door a *kick* to get it open.
She felt the baby's *kicks* all night.

gloss: A secret illegal payment made to someone in return for a favor or a contract.
examples: The inspector took *kickbacks* from three contractors.
Prosecutors say the deal involved a fifty-thousand-dollar *kickback*.
The company fired two managers over *kickbacks*.

ru: кикер (игрок, бьющий по мячу); неожиданный поворот
gloss: The player on a football team whose job is kicking the ball, or, informally, the surprising twist at the end of a story.
examples: Their *kicker* missed a field goal from thirty yards.
The team signed a rookie *kicker* in March.
And here's the *kicker* — he'd never driven a truck in his life.

gloss: A person who takes someone away by force and holds them, usually for money.
examples: The *kidnappers* demanded a million dollars.
A *kidnapper* was arrested at the border crossing.
Police believe the *kidnappers* knew the family.

gloss: An act of causing someone's death.
examples: The *killing* took place outside a bar downtown.
There have been four *killings* in the county this year.
He denied any part in the *killing*.

gloss: A unit of computer data equal to about a thousand bytes.
examples: The file is only forty *kilobytes*.
A page of plain text is a couple of *kilobytes*.
Back then a *kilobyte* of memory cost real money.

gloss: A pleated knee-length skirt of tartan cloth, traditionally worn by Scottish men.
examples: He wore a *kilt* to his sister's wedding.
The pipers all had matching *kilts*.
Every clan has its own tartan for its *kilts*.

gloss: A long loose Japanese robe with wide sleeves, tied with a sash.
examples: She was wearing a silk *kimono*.
The museum has a whole room of antique *kimonos*.
He pulled a *kimono* on over his pajamas.

gloss: A group of people or things that share the same qualities.
examples: What *kind* of dog is that?
They sell three *kinds* of bread.
I've never seen that *kind* of behavior from her.
contrast: *Kind* is countable and must agree: this kind of car, these kinds of cars — not "these kind of cars."

gloss: A country ruled by a king or a queen.
examples: Spain is still a *kingdom*.
The story is set in a small mountain *kingdom*.
The two *kingdoms* were joined by a marriage.

gloss: The most important person in a group or operation, especially a criminal one.
examples: The trial of the drug *kingpin* starts Monday.
He was the *kingpin* of a smuggling ring.
Two *kingpins* were extradited last year.

gloss: A tight bend or twist in something long, or a small problem in a plan or system.
examples: There's a *kink* in the hose.
We're still working the *kinks* out of the new system.
She had a *kink* in her neck from sleeping wrong.

gloss: Family relationship by blood or marriage, or a feeling of closeness to people like yourself.
examples: The study looks at *kinship* among herding families.
*Kinship* still decides who inherits the land there.
There was a real sense of *kinship* between the two crews.

gloss: A touch with the lips as a sign of love, affection, or greeting.
examples: She gave him a quick *kiss* on the cheek.
He blew a *kiss* from the train window.
The letter ended with a row of *kisses*.

gloss: A very small kitchen or cooking area inside a room or apartment.
examples: The studio has a *kitchenette* with a hot plate and a sink.
Both rooms come with a *kitchenette*.
There's a microwave in the *kitchenette* down the hall.

gloss: Pots, pans, and other equipment used for cooking.
examples: The store's *kitchenware* is on the second floor.
We registered for *kitchenware* and towels.
Most of our *kitchenware* came from a yard sale.
contrast: Uncountable: a piece of *kitchenware*, never "a kitchenware" or "kitchenwares."

gloss: A light frame covered with paper or cloth, flown in the wind on a long string.
examples: The kids flew a *kite* on the beach all afternoon.
His *kite* got caught in a tree.
There were dozens of *kites* over the park.

gloss: Art or decoration that is cheap, sentimental, and in poor taste.
examples: The whole diner is done up in fifties *kitsch*.
Some of it is real folk art and some of it is pure *kitsch*.
She collects Christmas *kitsch* from thrift stores.
contrast: The final -tsch is one sound, /tʃ/: KICH, rhyming with itch.

gloss: A mental condition in which a person cannot stop stealing things.
examples: His lawyer argued that he suffers from *kleptomania*.
*Kleptomania* has nothing to do with needing the money.
She's being treated for *kleptomania*.

gloss: A person who cannot stop themselves from stealing.
examples: Her uncle was a *kleptomaniac* who took silverware from restaurants.
The store detective said he'd caught the same *kleptomaniac* twice.
*Kleptomaniacs* often steal things they don't even want.

gloss: A clumsy person who is always dropping things or bumping into them.
examples: I'm such a *klutz* — I spilled it again.
He's a total *klutz* on the dance floor.
Only a *klutz* could break two glasses in one shift.

gloss: The sound of hitting something, especially a door, with your knuckles.
examples: There was a *knock* at the door around midnight.
He gave the window two sharp *knocks*.
I didn't hear your *knock*.
contrast: The k is silent: NAHK — the same silent k as in knee and knife.

gloss: A small round hill.
examples: The house sits on a grassy *knoll* above the river.
We ate lunch on a *knoll* overlooking the valley.
Low *knolls* run along the edge of the pasture.
contrast: The k is silent and the vowel is long: NOHL, rhyming with roll.

gloss: A small oval orange citrus fruit that is eaten whole, skin and all.
examples: She keeps a bowl of *kumquats* on the counter.
A *kumquat* is sour inside and sweet on the outside.
The tree by the porch is loaded with *kumquats*.

gloss: A deep cut or tear in the skin.
examples: He was treated for a *laceration* on his forehead.
The dog bite left three *lacerations*.
She had a *laceration* that needed eight stitches.

gloss: The state of not having something, or of not having enough of it.
examples: The project failed for *lack* of funding.
There's no *lack* of opinions around here.
Her decision showed a complete *lack* of judgment.
contrast: It takes *a* only in the pattern *a lack of something*: a lack of sleep, but never "many lacks."

gloss: The production of milk by a mother's body after she gives birth.
examples: The hospital has a *lactation* consultant on staff.
Some medications interfere with *lactation*.
*Lactation* usually begins within a few days of the birth.

gloss: A polite word for a woman.
examples: A *lady* at the counter helped me find it.
Two older *ladies* were waiting on the bench.
Ask that *lady* over there.
contrast: The plural changes y to ies: one lady, two ladies.

gloss: The land or property along the edge of a lake.
examples: They rented a cabin on the *lakefront*.
The city is rebuilding the path along the *lakefront*.
Most of the *lakefront* here is public park.

gloss: A Buddhist religious teacher in Tibet or Mongolia.
examples: The *lama* spoke to the students for an hour.
Several *lamas* took part in the ceremony.
He studied under a *lama* in Nepal.
contrast: One l here — a *llama* with two l's is the South American animal, though the two sound the same.

gloss: The eleventh letter of the Greek alphabet, written as a symbol in math, science, and programming.
examples: Wavelength is written with a *lambda*.
In the formula, *lambda* stands for the decay constant.
Python calls these little anonymous functions *lambdas*.

gloss: An expression of grief or complaint, in words or in music.
examples: The song is a *lament* for a lost brother.
You hear the same *lament* from every small farmer in the county.
Her column was a long *lament* about the state of the schools.

gloss: A spacecraft built to touch down on the surface of a planet or moon.
examples: The *lander* touched down near the south pole.
Both *landers* stopped transmitting after a week.
Engineers lost contact with the *lander* during its descent.

ru: выход на сушу (о шторме); подход к берегу
gloss: The moment when a storm or a ship first reaches land.
examples: The hurricane made *landfall* just south of Corpus Christi.
The storm is expected to make *landfall* Tuesday night.
They made *landfall* after nineteen days at sea.

gloss: A woman who rents out a room, an apartment, or a house to tenants.
examples: Our *landlady* lives on the first floor.
The *landlady* raised the rent again.
Both *landladies* wanted a deposit up front.

gloss: A large continuous area of land, such as a continent.
examples: Australia is the smallest continental *landmass*.
The two *landmasses* were once joined.
Ice once covered the northern half of the *landmass*.

gloss: A person who owns land, especially a large amount of it.
examples: The pipeline needs permission from every *landowner* along the route.
She's the biggest *landowner* in the county.
Local *landowners* opposed the plan.
